# Transforms and data morphs

::: {.doc-lead}
Move between views, change a plot’s data, or turn one object into another.
:::

<nav class="quick-path" aria-label="Choose a transform"><a href="#change">Change an object ↓</a><a href="#ghost">Create copies ↓</a><a href="#become">Become another object ↓</a></nav>

## Transforms {#transforms}

Choose a transform to match what you want to show:

| What you want to show | Use |
|---|---|
| Move, resize, recolour or rewrite an object | [Change](#change) |
| Bring an object back to how it looked earlier | [Return to an earlier look](#return-to-design) |
| Send independent copies out from one source | [Ghost](#ghost) |
| Turn an object into another object, plot parts or another plot | [Become](#become) |
| Zoom the camera toward something | [Camera](#camera-zoom-vs-fly) |
| Zoom, pan or rescale the data inside a plot | [Axis view](#axis-view-data-space-transforms) |
| Recolour a colour-mapped plot in data units | [Colour scale](#colour-scale-recolouring-in-data-units) |
| Let a plot take the deck's colours | [Plots follow the deck theme](#plots-follow-the-deck-theme) |

Change, Ghost and Become use the same [timing and easing controls](/docs/animation.html). An
object, or a specific set of plot parts, can have one transform per step; later steps can
transform it again, and chained transforms compose. While a transform is selected, **Before** and
**After** choose which of its two endpoints you edit. New transforms take 1.2 s on a Smooth curve
([Default timing](/docs/animation.html#default-timing)).

### Change {#change}

<div class="doc-study" data-doc-study="/demos/studies/change.html">
<div class="doc-study-stage"><img src="/demos/studies/change.svg" alt="233 seeds move from a nearby angle to the golden angle" width="1280" height="720" loading="lazy"><button class="doc-study-launch" type="button" data-study-start data-title="233 seeds move from a nearby angle to the golden angle" hidden><span aria-hidden="true">▶</span> Try this example</button></div>
<div class="doc-study-caption"><span class="study-label">Interactive example · a slide from the Flux film</span><p><strong>Keep the objects; change their state.</strong> Each of the 233 seeds is one object. One <strong>Change</strong> per seed moves the spiral to a nearby angle, which leaves gaps; the next moves it back to the golden angle, which fills the disc. Reduced motion shows each finished step.</p></div>
</div>


A **Change** animates an object into a different version of itself.

1. Select the object and choose **Transform ▸ Change** (**Ctrl+Shift+C**).
2. Edit its **After** state with the ordinary tools: move, resize, recolour or rewrite it.
3. Preview the step, then adjust its duration and easing in the Animator.

The bar above the stage tells you where edits go. **Before** selects the preceding step
(or Design for the first change); **After** selects the current step. Only the properties
you edit are recorded, so later changes build on earlier ones; colours blend perceptually, and
a rewritten number counts up in place. To stop overriding a property, remove it from the
Animation inspector’s **Δ** row. A closed shape that starts at another corner or winds the other
way no longer collapses on the way, and a path with a hole keeps its hole.

#### Rewrite text {#text-morph}

**Rewriting text** plays a *text morph*. Words the old and new text share glide from where
they were to where they land, even when they change order, case or style; a word that grows
into a longer one (*quick* → *quickly*, *Microscope* → *Microscopy*) glides and gains its new
letters on the way. Everything else fades: old letters lift away and fade in reading order while
the new ones rise in from below, so the line turns over left to right without ever going empty.
Crossing words fan out onto separate lanes so they stay readable, and a size, weight or colour
change travels with each word. A rewrite of more than 200 characters moves line by line. When a
text is rearranged into an anagram (*listen* → *silent*), its letters fly to their new places.
The line is the crisp resting text at both ends of the move.

Two options on a text Change in the Animator set this look, and both are on for every new text
Change: **Letters travel** (an anagram's letters fly to their partners) and **Fade style** —
**Roll** (leftover words lift away and rise in by about a third of the text height) or **Drift**
(the older look: a fade with a small nudge and scale). Saved decks play as they were made.

#### Connectors and labels follow what they stick to {#connectors-follow}

When a shape moves at a step — by a Change, an arc or a spring — the arrows and labels stuck to
it move with it, in the editor, in Present and in every export, and a moving label glides
without stepping. Sticking works exactly as in Figure: release a line end on a shape, or set the
Inspector's **Sticks to** row ([Align and arrange on the stage](/docs/slides.html#align-and-arrange-on-slides)).
Dragging a shape at a step writes the shape's Change only; a Change of a stuck label's own
position is ignored, and an issue says so. A connector stuck to a shape that hands off in a
Become stays where it rests. Plot parts and groups are not things to stick to. A deck that holds
a stuck element is saved in a newer format, which older versions of Flux do not open.

```bash
flux slide-attach talk slide1 arrow1 --start box1 --end box2      # a connector follows two shapes
flux slide-attach talk slide1 label1 --to box1 --side n --gap 8   # a label sits above a shape
flux slide-attach talk slide1 label1 --detach
```

`--start` and `--end` take `<id>[:anchor[:gap]]`, with anchor `auto` (aims at the other end),
`center`, `n`, `e`, `s`, `w` or `fx,fy`; a label takes `--to <id> --side n|e|s|w`, `--gap` and
`--align center|start|end`. `figure-attach` takes the same arguments on a Figure canvas.

#### Bend the path: Arc, Suggest arcs and Turn {#arc}

For a box move, the **Arc** slider bends the path to either side of the straight line.
Zero keeps it straight; the endpoints stay fixed. The small path preview shows the bend.
Arc shares the transform's easing and can be inherited from an animation style. A Become's
flying pieces bend by it too (letters, shattered pieces, text and 3D models fly straight).

**Suggest arcs** gives the moves of the current step that would pass through each other an
arc — the smallest of 0.25, 0.45 and 0.83 (manim's 90° swap) that clears them — as one Undo. It
leaves alone any move whose arc you have set, including an explicit 0.

For a line or a straight connector, **Turn** chooses how it moves when its ends change:
**Shrink** (the default: its ends move straight, so it shortens while it turns and stays joined
to what it connects) or **Rigid** (it keeps its length, like a rotating arrow).

```bash
flux set-transform talk slide1 step1 object1 --state '{"x":420,"y":160}' --arc 0.5
flux set-transform talk slide1 step1 arrow1 --turn rigid    # on the arrow's Change at this step
flux suggest-arcs talk slide1 step1
```

<!-- MEDIA: Two boxes that swap places: straight paths pass through each other, then Suggest arcs bends them apart. -->

#### Return to an earlier look {#return-to-design}

**Return to Design** (in **Transform ▾**, or right-click a Change) brings an object back to how
it looked at Design, as an ordinary Change at this step; **Return to before step N** brings it
back to how it looked before that step. If the step already has a Change for the object, its
other settings stay, and Flux tells you which of them the return replaced. A return is refused
when the object's content has changed since then (a Become, a new plot).

```bash
flux restore-state talk slide1 step3 object1 --to 0              # back to Design
flux restore-state talk slide1 step3 object1 --to 2 --keys x,y   # back to its place before step 2
```

#### Resize a plot {#plot-resize-changes}

A Change that resizes a plot saved by fluxplot ≥ 0.4 **reflows** it: the axes resize while
text, strokes and markers keep their physical sizes, and tick sets crossfade when the new size
needs different ticks. Dense plots use a fast preview and settle to the exact layout at the
endpoint; exported presentations use the same layout. The plot's **Layout** controls in the
Object inspector (**Reflow** or **Stretch**) decide which happens, and the status line beneath
them names the reason for a layout that cannot reflow (see the Figure guide,
[Layout, drawing and typography](/docs/figure-layout.html)). A plot saved by an older fluxplot
stretches until it is regenerated.

### Ghost {#ghost}

<div class="doc-study" data-doc-study="/demos/studies/ghost.html">

<div class="doc-study-caption"><span class="study-label">Interactive example · a slide from the Flux film</span><p><strong>One source, independent copies.</strong> Every projection of the three disks leaves a <strong>Ghost</strong> that travels into the sinogram, one angle per step. In the last step the same copies sweep back through the object to form an unfiltered backprojection. Exact projections, computed. Use the next-step arrow to play; reset to watch again. Reduced motion shows each finished step.</p></div>

**Transform ▸ Ghost…** creates independent copies that move out from an object. For example,
one arrow can split into three arrows pointing to three new results.

1. Select the source object and the step where the copies should appear, then choose
   **Transform ▸ Ghost…**.
2. Choose the number of copies (1–32; initially 3) and whether the original should **Stay**,
   **Disappear**, or **Transform** too.
3. Create the ghosts. Flux selects the first copy in **Edit after step**. Move, resize,
   rotate, restyle, or edit it with the ordinary tools to set its destination — or make it
   **Become** something else (below).
4. Use the copy selector and Previous/Next controls to edit the other copies, even while
   they overlap. **Add copy** adds another destination; **Select original** returns to the source.
5. Play the step. Each copy begins at the original's state at the end of the preceding step
   and moves to its own destination. Adjust each lane's delay, duration, and easing normally.

Ghosts are identical copies when they start; they have normal opacity unless you change it.
Changes to the original in earlier steps update their starting state. A transform of the original
in the same step runs independently. The copies remain available for further animations in later steps.

Before their creation step, ghosts are absent, including with **Show hidden** enabled. Use
**Edit destination** to return to the step where a selected ghost can be edited. Deleting a
ghost's creation lane removes that copy and its later effects; Undo restores them together.

### Become {#become}

<div class="doc-study" data-doc-study="/demos/studies/become.html">
<div class="doc-study-stage"><img src="/demos/studies/become.svg" alt="The dots of the Flux mark become shapes and a caption" width="1280" height="720" loading="lazy"><button class="doc-study-launch" type="button" data-study-start data-title="The dots of the Flux mark become shapes and a caption" hidden><span aria-hidden="true">▶</span> Try this example</button></div>
<div class="doc-study-caption"><span class="study-label">Interactive example · a slide from the Flux film</span><p><strong>Objects become other objects.</strong> The 88 dots of a plotted Flux mark <strong>Become</strong> five shapes, a frame and a caption, and each letter flies out of a dot. This is the slide made live in the Flux film: select the dots, press <strong>B</strong>, pick the targets. Use the next-step arrow to play; reset to watch again. Reduced motion shows each finished step.</p></div>
</div>


**Transform ▸ Become** (or just **B** with something selected) makes an object
become another object or part of a plot. Select the source first. To start from plot parts,
**Ctrl+click** a part or pick several rows in the **X-ray** before arming Become.

1. Select the source, then press **B**.
2. Pick what it should become. Double-click for a single destination, or select several and press **Enter**.
3. Preview the step. Adjust its duration and easing in the Animation inspector.

<details class="doc-details"><summary>Picker shortcuts and selecting several targets</summary>

Choosing Become enters the **Become picker**, a temporary mode. The slide wears a soft green
outline, the canvas around it dims slightly, the source gets a dashed green outline, and the bar
above the canvas names what is waiting (**‹Rect› becomes…**). Nothing is moved or edited while
picking: every click on the canvas is a pick.

- **Hover** outlines the finest thing under the pointer: a single point, bar, box, tick or
  label of a plot, or one member of a group. The bar names it exactly as its timeline lane will,
  with the point's data where it has one.
- **Click** picks it. Picking is always multi-select: keep clicking to add more, and click a
  picked thing again to remove it. Picks wear a solid green outline (a ring around round marks),
  numbered in picking order when there are few of them; the bar lists them as chips
  (**6 points · W1**, **2 ellipses**) that you can remove with ×.
- **Drag** anywhere on the stage to draw a box: it picks everything **fully inside**. Data marks
  win over ticks and labels; a whole object inside the box is picked whole. **Alt+drag**
  removes what it encloses.
- **Alt+click** picks the whole plot or group instead of the part. **A** widens the last pick to
  its siblings: the other members of its group, then the same part of every series, then the
  rest of its series. **Backspace** drops the last pick.
- **Double-click** picks something and confirms at once, the quick path for a single object.
- **Space**, **Enter** or the **Become** button confirms. **Escape** or **Cancel** leaves the picker
  without creating a transform and puts the source selection back. Changing slides or steps also
  cancels.
- **Add mode** lets the source become something that does not exist yet. Press a drawing tool
  key (**Alt+R** rect, **O** ellipse, **L** line, **P** pen, **T** text), **Ctrl+P** for a preset,
  place a plot from the [Plots rail](/docs/slides.html#the-plots-rail) (**Alt+G**, or
  **Add ▾ → Plot…**), or choose from **Add ▾** on the bar. The outline gains an inner
  dashed line and the editor works as usual: everything you draw or insert joins the pick.
  **Enter** or **Done** returns to picking with those objects picked; **Escape** also returns,
  and a second **Escape** cancels.
- **X-ray**: hover a plot and press **R** (**Shift+Alt+R** adds the picks' families). Rows you
  select join the pick and rows you clear leave it, live on the canvas; points picked on the
  canvas stay picked. Axis rows include their spine, ticks and labels; expand them to choose only
  the spine. **Space** (or **B**) in the X-ray confirms the whole pick, and closing the X-ray
  keeps it.

- **Several things at once.** Pick several things and the source becomes **all of them**: three
  loose ellipses, parts of two different plots, or a mix of shapes and plot parts. Your layers stay
  as they are; there is no need to group anything first (**Alt+click** a grouped object to pick its
  whole group). The source's outline splits into one piece per destination, and each piece lands
  exactly on its own object. The lane and the Destination row name the set (**Rect → 3 ellipses**)
  and list its members; a set cannot be swapped — author the reverse hand-offs from each object.
  The pieces fly together by default; the Animator's **Piece lag** slider makes them **peel off
  one after another**, in reading order, inside the same duration (a bar splitting into five dots
  then reads as five dots leaving, not one slab breaking).

</details>

A Become completes in one of two ways:

- **Consume** applies when one whole drawn object becomes another. The destination's appearance
  becomes the source's After state and the destination is removed; the source keeps its
  identity. One Undo restores both.
- **Hand-off** applies to plots, images, groups and part sets. Both objects stay in the slide:
  the destination is hidden until the source lands, and the source is hidden afterwards. For
  example, a drawn chevron can become a plot's X and Y axis spines, or a box in a plot can
  become a rectangle.

When the source and the destination sit on different sides of an object the flight crosses (one
above it, one below), the flying shape sinks under that object, or rises out of it, over the whole
flight instead of jumping behind or in front of it on the first frame.

After you confirm, the canvas switches to **Edit after step**, with the new track selected in
the **Animation** inspector; **Show hidden** shows the hidden side as a faint ghost. Groups and
sets of several objects can be destinations, but the source must be one object or a set of plot
parts. A set always hands off, because **Consume** and **↔ Swap direction** need a single
destination. Video clips cannot take part in a Become; use Change to move or resize them.

**Appear from…** works from the other end. Select the destination object or plot parts (or
several objects, which then appear together from one source) and choose
**Appear ▾ → Appear from…** (**Ctrl+Alt+A**); the main **Appear** button still adds a normal
entrance. The same picker opens, and the bar names what **appears from…**. Pick the source and
confirm with **Space** or **Enter**, or double-click it. In the X-ray, press **M**, then **5**
(**Appear from…**) to start the same flow from the picked rows. Both routes create the same
hand-off.

**Merge many into one.** Pick several sources and confirm: each source gets its own hand-off
into the same destination, all in one Undo. The destination is shared out among them (the
reverse of becoming a set). The pieces converge, a piece that arrives early waits in place, and
the destination appears when the last one lands. Each source keeps its own lane, so you can
stagger them.

**Pair** chooses how the outlines match: **auto**, **by position**, **by order**, **by data**,
or **tile**. Connected strokes, such as two axis spines, form one path. Order follows point
indices; tile divides one outline among its partners. By data lands points at their values
on the destination axis. This supports **data ↔ summary**: points can become a distribution,
or a summary can expand back into its points. Unmatched sources fade out; unmatched
parts of the destination fade in. Images crossfade while their boxes move.

**How a shape changes shape.** Convex shapes round off progressively (a square becomes a circle
without a cushion at the corners), a line swells into the shape, and an arrowhead rides the tip
as it melts. Dashed outlines keep their dash rhythm, and translucent and colormap-filled shapes
keep their paint throughout. Shapes with a dent (a star, an L, a pen shape) keep the older, more
organic morph, so one slide can mix both looks. A shape with corners keeps its sharp corners,
stroke included, until they round off; an arrow's body starts inside its head; a donut closes
its hole as it becomes a disc. Several objects becoming one (or one becoming several) fly to
their places without crossing, and a crossfade between two boxes keeps full strength instead of
dipping.

**Text and shapes.** When a shape becomes text, it splits into one piece per letter, in
reading order, and each piece pours into its letter's outline. When text becomes a shape,
the letters fuse into it. A text that becomes another text plays the [text morph](#text-morph)
described under Change, whether by Consume or by hand-off. Letter outlines come from the font
installed on your computer, and an exported presentation carries the outlines of the
letters it needs. When no outline is readable, the letters land as rounded boxes and then
fade into the text, and the Animation inspector reports it. This happens with the bundled
Gelasio typeface or in a browser preview without the desktop app.

After a hand-off to some of a plot's parts, when the plot has no appearance effects yet,
the toast offers **Auto-animate the rest…**. It adds the plot's remaining build phases after
the landing, excluding the leaves already revealed by the hand-off. A hand-off to the whole
plot already reveals every part, so it offers no remainder.

**Destination.** The Animation inspector names both sides of a hand-off; for a set it reads,
for example, “hands off to 3 ellipses” and lists each member below. Its controls:

- **Pair ▾** chooses auto, by position, by order, by data or tile; **Reveal** chooses flip or draw.
- **Method ▾** chooses what a filled shape's interior does while its outline splits into
  several pieces (or several pieces merge into it). **Dissolve**, the default, fades it away in
  place as the outline leaves; **shatter** splits it into wedges that fly with the pieces;
  **collapse** shrinks it into the shape's centre; **drain** empties it toward where the pieces
  are going (and fills from that side when pieces merge). A shape becoming letters always pours
  its area into them.
- **Piece lag** (0–1) makes the pieces of a hand-off peel off one after another in reading order
  within the same duration; 0, the default, flies them together.
- **↔ Swap direction** reverses the hand-off, including plot parts, in one Undo, keeping timing,
  styles and follower links. It is unavailable for a ghost's creation, a group source, a missing
  outline, or a destination that already has a transform in this step. The command twin is
  `swap-become`.
- **Consume instead**, for whole loose objects, asks for a second click before it removes the
  destination.
- **Auto-animate the rest…** builds the destination plot's remaining parts after the hand-off.
  Like the toast, it appears only for a hand-off to some of the plot's parts.
- **Become** picks a different destination for this effect.

<!-- MEDIA: A bar hands off to five dots: once with Piece lag 0 (one slab breaking), once with Piece lag 0.3 (the pieces peel off left to right). -->

With a whole plot as the source, **From gallery…** keeps its frame and changes its content
to another project plot. **Data from gallery…** and **Keep own data** in the Animation
inspector edit or remove that content target. Shared supported series tween in data space;
a series without a tweenable counterpart fades on its own, and only an SVG without semantic
IDs crossfades as a whole. A Become at a step with an existing Change replaces that
same target's endpoint; a ghost can Become something at its birth step.

From the command line or an agent, `become` creates the same transforms, and `appear-from`
authors them from the destination's side:

- `--part` names destination parts and `--source-part` names source parts.
- A destination set is `--to <id>` repeated, or `--members` with a JSON list of objects and their
  parts. `appear-from --members` likewise reveals a destination set from one source.
- Plots, images and part sets hand off by default, and whole drawn objects use Consume;
  `--mode` chooses either completion for whole objects.
- `--pair` chooses how outlines match, `--reveal` chooses flip or draw, and
  `--method dissolve|shatter|collapse|drain` chooses what a filled shape's interior does.
- `appear-from --pair-lag 0..1` sets the piece lag of a new hand-off; `set-track --pair-lag`
  edits it later.

See the [slide command reference](/docs/commands.html#slide-commands) for the full syntax.

In the Slides workspace, **Plots & videos** (or **Shift+Alt+G**) opens the same
[Plot gallery](/docs/plot-gallery.html#getting-plots-in) that Figure uses, with adjustable preview
sizes, spacing and names and a **Pin open** button that keeps it in a separate window for inserting
several plots. **Alt+G** shows the [Plots rail](/docs/slides.html#the-plots-rail) beside the stage
instead.

### Camera: Zoom vs Fly {#camera-zoom-vs-fly}

**Zoom** adds a camera move toward the selected object; **Reset** pulls back to the full slide.
When plot parts are drilled, **Zoom** frames their combined outline instead of the whole plot.
After-step editing uses the same camera mapping, so selection, dragging, and highlights stay aligned.

Select a camera track in the Animator to choose **Path: Zoom | Fly**. **Zoom** is the default:
the view expands or contracts about a fixed point, at a constant proportional zoom rate before
easing. With no zoom change, it pans in a straight line. **Fly** pulls back for a long pan,
travels, then moves in toward the destination. Its **suggested … ms** hint shows a duration
based on the distance and zoom change; click **Apply** to use it. You can still edit duration
and easing yourself.

Camera tracks created in earlier versions of Flux also use the Zoom path now. Their start and
end views are unchanged, but the frames in between differ, and there is no option to restore the
old path.

### Axis view: data-space transforms {#axis-view-data-space-transforms}

**Axis view** edits a plot's data view, which records its x/y limits and linear or log scales. A Change of this view
zooms, pans or rescales the data inside the plot; the plot's position and size can change at
the same time. A ghost can therefore float away while zooming into a smaller data range.
A saved view also applies in the Figure workspace, Paper embeds and exports.

Lines, points, bars, heatmap cells, hexagons, contour bands and box or violin bodies move
through the new axis mapping. During the glide the ticks, gridlines and tick labels glide to
their new values: ticks that exist at both ends walk, ticks that only the old view has leave and
ticks that only the new view has arrive (they never coexist), and a label that is re-formatted
for the same value ("1" to "1.0") swaps once. The last frame is exactly the viewed axis,
re-ticked for its new limits. Categories, dates and fixed labels keep their own ticks, which move
with their data values and fade near the edges. A log view requires positive limits and positive
data; an unsupported series keeps its original geometry and the animation reports why. Images
and rasterized layers keep their geometry. A twin value axis (`y2` / `x2`, recorded from fluxplot
schema 0.3.2) has its own limits in the view.

A plot needs a manifest with series and calibrated axes. Unsupported axes stay disabled with
a reason. Select a plot and use **Axis view** in the Object inspector, or **x view** / **y view** in
its **F** menu. Enter limits in data units; empty fields use the generated limits shown as
placeholders. Choose **linear** or **log**, or **Reset** both axes. At **After step N** the
edit becomes a Change on that step, with one undo per edit. Scrubbing previews the axis glide.
X-ray's axis-row **v · Axis view…** focuses the matching Inspector row.

On axes that keep their own ticks, ticks exactly on a new limit fade to zero (the outer 4%
rule). Non-series marks, such as a dashed reference line, stay put. For multi-panel plots the
same view applies to each panel; placeholders show the first panel's limits.

Becomes between plots and Changes of a data view use the same projection, so one Change may
combine new data, axis limits and movement. Every mark travels in a straight line from where it
sits in the first plot to where it sits in the second, even when the new version changes the
axis's units or scale (a log ratio axis to percentage points); mean dots and outliers keep their
size. When the two versions tick an axis at different values, the old ticks ride the moving axis
and fade out while the new ones fade in. Shared semantic parts tween; removed parts fade out in
the first 40% and added parts fade in during the last 40%. A chained Change starts from exactly
the plot the step before it left.

From fluxplot schema 0.3.2, bars carry stable keys by category, and heatmap cells and hexagons
by row and column. Between two versions of such a plot, each member tweens to its namesake: a
bar grows or shrinks to its new height, and a hexagon's colour passes through the colour scale
at the intermediate value. A bar that exists in only one version grows from, or shrinks onto,
its own baseline instead of fading. A bar chart or a hexmatrix with new data can therefore be a
Become even without lines or points.

A local change in the SVG structure fades that part, and an SVG without semantic IDs crossfades
as a whole. Matching ignores positional IDs (matplotlib's numbered `ytick_7`-style IDs and the
ones Flux stamps), so a tick keeps its identity when a regenerated plot renumbers them, and the
last frame is exactly the new plot.

The CLI/MCP twin is **set-plot-view** / **set_plot_view**:

```bash
flux set-plot-view figure1 plot1 --x-min 0 --x-max 10
flux set-plot-view talk/slide1 plot1 --y-min 1 --y-max 100 --y-scale log \
  --beat beat2
flux set-plot-view talk/slide1 plot1 --reset --beat beat3
```

With a figure as the target, the command saves the view on the object. With a deck/slide target
and no `--beat`, it edits the Design object; with `--beat`, it writes a Change's `state.view` at
that step, preserving other changed properties and inheriting earlier limits. `--reset` restores
the generated axes.

### Plots follow the deck theme {#plots-follow-the-deck-theme}

A plot saved with fluxplot schema 0.3.1 or later tags every piece of its scaffold — tick labels, titles,
ticks, spines, gridlines, backgrounds — with the theme token it was drawn in. On a slide the
plot **follows the deck theme** by default: its ink takes the theme's text colour, its axes the
muted text, its gridlines a faint mix of text into the background, and its backgrounds turn
transparent, so a plot saved on white reads on *Flux Dark* without a regeneration. Data colours
never change. **Follow deck theme** in the Object inspector turns it off for one plot (a plot
whose white ground is the point). Copies of the plot in the Figure workspace and Paper keep their
generated ink: there is no deck theme to follow there.

### Colour scale: recolouring in data units {#colour-scale-recolouring-in-data-units}

A colour-mapped plot saved with fluxplot schema 0.3.1 or later carries **Colour scales**,
element state like the axis view: the palette, its direction, the norm kind, the limits and
`extend`. A Change
of a colour scale repaints every coloured element and the key's gradient and ticks through the
data values, so one step can narrow a heatmap's range, switch a hexbin to a log scale or swap its
colormap while the plot moves. Limits glide (log limits in log space), a new palette blends table
by table, a changed norm kind switches at the midpoint. A saved scale also applies in the Figure
workspace, Paper embeds and exports.

Select the plot and edit **Colour scales** in the Object inspector. At **After step N** the edit
becomes a Change on that step, with one undo per edit; scrubbing the Animator previews the glide.
A scale drawn as one raster image cannot recolour live and reports itself.

The CLI/MCP twin is **set-plot-color-scale** / **set_plot_color_scale**;
**get-plot-color-scales** / **get_plot_color_scales** lists a plot's scales, what may change
and the live view a figure, a Design or a step holds:

```bash
flux set-plot-color-scale figure1 plot1 --cmap crameri.batlow --vmax 20
flux set-plot-color-scale talk/slide1 plot1 --norm log --vmin 1 --vmax 100 \
  --beat beat2
flux set-plot-color-scale talk/slide1 plot1 --reset --beat beat3
flux set-plot-color-scale figure1 plot1 --scale rates --cmap magma --regenerate
flux get-plot-color-scales talk/slide1 plot1 --beat beat2
```

With a figure as the target, the command saves the scale on the object; `--regenerate` also
writes the complete `__fluxplot__` control into the recipe, re-runs it, refreshes the figure and
clears the live edit. With a deck/slide target and no `--beat`, it edits the Design object; with
`--beat` it writes `state.colorScale` at that step, inheriting earlier edits. `--scale` names the
scale when a plot has several. Omitted fields are preserved, and `--reset` restores the generated
scale.

**set-series-color** / **set_series_color** gives a whole series one colour on a slide's Design:

```bash
flux set-series-color talk/slide1 counts '#205ea6' --element plot1
```

To check colour choices, **View as…** in the toolbar previews the stage as a colour-deficient
audience sees it (see [View as](/docs/plot-editing.html#view-as)).
